extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Tatler / polite London public interested in manners, conduct, and social critique
extracted.subtask_description: Short early-18th-century essays discussing standards of speech, civility, and the customs and ethics of duelling, with illustrative anecdotes and prescriptive judgments about social behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of speech / avoid roaring
rubrics_metrics.description: One that disturbs but a room or a family is more to be tolerated, than one who draws together parishes and counties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loud, intrusive speech that gathers crowds or causes public disturbance. Example/anecdote: Mr. Bellfrey 'struck up a fox-chase' in a drawing-room, causing a dog to bark, china to be thrown down and general confusion — an instance of roaring instead of speaking and of speech used where silence or ordinary speech would be proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities for a whispering maid (servant for a gentlewoman)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentlewoman who has a very delicate ear, wants a maid who can whisper, and help her in the government of her family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical desired qualities: clear-starch, lisp, and tread softly. The text states: 'If the said servant can clear-starch, lisp, and tread softly, she shall have suitable encouragement in her wages.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of public papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of all public papers ought to be the benefit and instruction, as well as the diversion, of the readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public writing should instruct and benefit readers as well as entertain them. The author cites his writings' role in 'rooting out from amongst us that unchristianlike and bloody custom of duelling' as an example of beneficial public purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-lethal satisfaction for quarrels
rubrics_metrics.description: When honour demands satisfaction, combat need not involve deadly weapons; a fair, non-lethal contest can settle matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by a true story: two officers, instead of shedding blood, 'stripped, and in decent manner fought full fairly with their wrathful hands' until one cried, 'I am satisfied, enough,' and peace followed. Encourages alternatives to lethal duels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds for drawing a sword
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man that drew his sword, unless in the Service, or purely to defend his life, person, or goods, from violence (I mean abstracted from all punctos or whims of honour) should be punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dueling or drawing a sword is justified only for military Service or genuine self-defence of life, person, or goods; not for punctilios of honour. Mr. Sage proposes severe societal punishments for unwarranted duelling (ridicule, pillory, confinement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duels and military reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A rencounter or duel was so far from being in fashion among the officers that served in the Parliament army, that on the contrary, it was as disreputable, and as great an impediment to advancement in the Service, as being bashful in time of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among some military cultures (here: Parliament army), duelling damages reputation and career prospects; military officers should avoid duels to maintain standing and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and transparency in duels
rubrics_metrics.description: That's true, sir; for the weapons were always equal. ... the principals put on their pumps, and stripped to their shirts, to show they had nothing but what men of honour carry about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules intended to ensure equality and transparency in single combat: equal weapons, visible persons (stripping to shirts) to show no hidden advantages. These are meant to make a contest 'upon the square.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of seconds in duels
rubrics_metrics.description: They used seconds, who were to see that all was upon the square, and make a faithful report of the whole combat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seconds are meant as impartial witnesses to ensure fair play and to report the conduct/outcome truthfully. However, the essay also traces the danger that seconds may themselves become combatants, undermining the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of seconds engaging (anti‑pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a little time it became a fashion for the seconds to fight ... Major Adroit desired that the other second ... would try a thrust or two only to keep them warm ... who presently whipped Adroit through the body, disarmed him, and then parted the principals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing seconds to engage (even to 'keep warm') escalates conflicts and is an anti-pattern that transforms a controlled duel into broader, more dangerous fighting; historical example given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yield rule in duels (concession upon first disarm/kill)
rubrics_metrics.description: It was a law among the combatants, that the party which happened to have the first man disarmed or killed, should yield as vanquished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rule designed to limit bloodshed: if one side first has a man disarmed or killed, that side yields. This rule helped to curb endless fighting but also influenced fashions and notions of honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weapon choice to address disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: If an active, adroit, strong man, had insulted an awkward, or a feeble, or an unpractised swordsman ... Then, sir, they fought with pistols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching weapons (e.g., to pistols) was used historically to mitigate physical advantage in swordsmanship, though it raises its own issues about fairness and risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness as prerequisite for honour
rubrics_metrics.description: I am of opinion, that one can get no honour in killing a man ... when they have a trick to make the game secure, though they seem to play upon the square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A killing obtained through tricks or manipulations that secure an unfair outcome cannot be regarded as honourable; procedures that mask unfair advantage negate the honor of victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral judgment on killing in duels
rubrics_metrics.description: In truth, Mr. Sage, I think such a fact must be murder in a man's own private conscience, whatever it may appear to the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when socially condoned, taking a life in duel may be judged morally as murder by the actor's private conscience; public appearance does not erase private moral culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic/non‑lethal combat as honorable alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: I have known some men so nice, that they would not fight but upon a cloak without pistols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorses symbolic or minimal-contact forms of settlement (e.g., mock combat on a cloak) as ways to preserve honour without bloodshed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of vanity and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: In all their actions there is a secret approbation, either in the tone of their voice, the turn of their body, or cast of their eye, which shows that they are extremely in their own favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying impertinent, vain, or affected persons by observable cues: voice tone, body posture, and eye movements. Examples include the 'pretender to business' who seeks public notice and whispers secrets to feel important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic business vs pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: A pretender to business is never in secret, but in public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True men of business conduct important matters without performative public display; those who constantly make business public are likely pretenders seeking attention rather than actually busy or useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess people by intention
rubrics_metrics.description: If therefore it be a just rule to judge of a man by his intention, according to the equity of good breeding, he that is impertinently kind or wise, to do you service, ought in return to have a proportionable place both in your affection and esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating someone's conduct, consider their intentions: impertinent kindness motivated by good intent merits proportionate affection and esteem rather than pure disdain for its awkward form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to impotent malice
rubrics_metrics.description: Impotent malice is to be treated with all our force to depress it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malicious but weak actions (gossip, petty slander) should be actively opposed and socially sanctioned. Example: the character 'Flyblow' who spreads the worst of others' reputations should be treated as a knave despite his weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic markers of malice/character (overuse of 'but')
rubrics_metrics.description: You may know him by the frequency of pronouncing the particle 'but'; for which reason I never hear him spoke of with common charity, without using my 'but' against him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain linguistic habits (constant corrective 'but') are diagnostic of a tendency to diminish or spoil compliments and indicate a captious or malicious temper; use of such markers can guide social judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate dullness as rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to be noted, that when any part of this paper appears dull, there is a design in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may deliberately include passages that seem dull as an intentional device; readers should not assume lack of purpose when encountering such moments in the essay.
